newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: East European NATO applicants wary of summit deal.
newsitem.headline: East European NATO applicants wary of summit deal.

text.p: East European states seeking NATO membership are anxious that key decisions might be taken in their absence at a U.S.-Russian summit next week, but they see no chance of alliance enlargement plans being derailed.
NATO's proposals for eastward expansion, bitterly opposed by Moscow, will top the agenda when Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin meet in Helsinki on March 19 and 20.
The post-communist states, though sensitive to Russia's security concerns, oppose any deal which would affect their prospects of membership or status within the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

"Poland firmly opposes such Russian demands towards NATO, the meeting of which would mean giving Poland a limited membership in the North Atlantic alliance," Poland's PAP news agency quoted Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati as saying.

The East European applicants, many of whom used to face NATO tanks and aircraft as members of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact, hope the summit will give new impetus to their bids to join but also that Russia's fears can be allayed.

"Russia is still a political and military great power and has to find a suitable place in the European security system. This will be at the centre of the negotiations at the summit," Hungarian Defence Minister Gyorgy Keleti told Reuters.
Would-be NATO members have made clear they want their voices heard on enlargement but do not see the Helsinki summit as affecting the alliance's resolve to expand.
"Helsinki will not mean that Russia will approve the enlargement or that NATO will say 'we withdraw our decision'," Czech Deputy Foreign Minister Karel Kovanda said last week.

Political analyst Jiri Pehe of Prague's Open Media Research Institute (OMRI) said most East European states sought NATO membership as a symbolic integration with the West rather than because of a perceived security threat.
"What matter is not whether Russia will be involved but how. If a deal is done with Russia without any consultation with the Central Europeans, it will anger some of them."
NATO will issue invitations for membership talks after an alliance summit in Madrid in July.
The leading candidates are the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary but Romania and Slovenia are also being discussed.

"Slovenia is especially interested in the result of this meeting because it expects to eb invited to take place in the first round of NATO enlargement," Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler told Reuters in a written statement this week.
Bulgaria and Slovakia also want to be in the first wave.
Romania, with the backing of Spain, France and Italy, has intensified diplomatic efforts to be among the first wave invited to join the alliance, even if it is accepted later.
Romanian President Emil Constantinescu, visiting Prague this week, said his country fulfilled all criteria of NATO membership except an ability to pay for upgrading its military.
"That is why we speak of Romania's nomination in the first wave followed by the effective integration when all the conditions would be fulfilled," he said.

Czech President Vaclav Havel, speaking after talks with Constantinescu, said NATO should have a clear timetable for membership for all suitable applicants and that the efforts to join the alliance should not be seen as a competition.
"(NATO) should give certainty to all in the spirit of the Washington Treaty, give hope to everybody and explain the logic of the potential schedule for its enlargement," Havel said.
"The point is for NATO to be an alliance open to all democratic countries in the Euro-Atlantic area," he said.
Slovakia is seen increasingly unlikely to make the first wave after repeated U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
"Our entire foreign policy and activity...is aimed at Slovakia becoming a member of NATO, foreign ministry spokesman Ivan Korcok said.
However, OMRI's Pehe said that leaving out Slovakia, or Romania, would be a mistake because of large Hungarian ethnic minorities in those countries.
"If you accept only the mother country, Hungary, you create a political problem and may create more instability than stability," he said.
